# Physical centroidal-cap concavity, equality, and deepest-point strata

Throughout the ordinary assertions, d>=1 and volume means d-dimensional
Lebesgue measure. For a convex body K and y in int K define

 T_K(y)=sup{integral_K f: 0<=f<=1,
                          integral_K (x-y)f(x)dx=0}.                 (1)

The density is a measurable function; zero is allowed. This is physical
retained mass, not projective energy or a density allowed to exceed one.

**Theorem A (joint concavity and exact equality).** Let lambda_i>0 sum
to one, let K_i be convex bodies, y_i in int K_i, and let K be a convex
body containing sum_i lambda_i K_i. Set y=sum_i lambda_i y_i. Then

 T_K(y)^(1/d) >= sum_i lambda_i T_(K_i)(y_i)^(1/d).                  (2)

Each maximum in (1) is the indicator of a unique convex cap D_K(y),
up to null sets, and that cap has centroid y. Equality in (2) holds if
and only if the caps D_i=D_(K_i)(y_i) are positively homothetic and

                 D_K(y)=sum_i lambda_i D_i.                       (3)

More precisely, writing s_i=|D_i|^(1/d), equality is equivalent to

 D_i=y_i+s_i D_0 for every i,   |D_0|=1,   g_(D_0)=0,
 D_K(y)=y+(sum_i lambda_i s_i)D_0.                                 (4)

**Theorem B (fixed-body strict quasiconcavity).** If y_1!=y_2 are in
int K and 0<lambda<1, then

 T_K((1-lambda)y_1+lambda y_2)>min(T_K(y_1),T_K(y_2)).               (5)

The root in (2) need not be strictly concave, even for a fixed simplex.
Equality controls the retained caps, not the entire input bodies.

Section 6 gives a mixed consequence with all ambient halfspaces: on
the actual deepest set, maximize the physical invariant T. There is
then at most one selected point in each fiber. At every integer-anchored
barycentric relation between selected points, the retained caps are
translates. Consequently at most 2^n retained-cap translation classes
occur. This is a structural theorem, with no asserted OC mass payment.

## 1. Exact attainment, unique density, and the cap

Here is the needed attainment argument, also proved in
`candidate 49e262af8d182671`.
Translate y to zero. The finite convex function

                    G(u)=integral_K (1+u.x)_+ dx

is coercive: an inner ball rB centered at zero gives
G(u)>=integral_(rB)(u.x)_+dx=c(d,r)||u|| with c(d,r)>0.
It is C1 by dominated differentiation; for nonzero u the exceptional
hyperplane 1+u.x=0 is null, while near u=0 the integrand is positive on K.
Its gradient is

                  grad G(u)=integral_(K intersect {1+u.x>=0}) x dx.

Let u_* minimize G and D=K intersect {1+u_*.x>=0}. The cap contains an
inner ball centered at zero, and stationarity gives g_D=0. Therefore
G(u_*)=|D|. For every feasible f in (1),

 integral_K f=integral_K (1+u_*.x)f <=G(u_*)=|D|.                  (6)

The indicator 1_D attains equality. Equality in (6) forces f=1 on the
positive side and f=0 on the negative side, almost everywhere. When
u_*=0 this says f=1 on all K. Thus the optimizing density is unique
a.e.; its convex body D is unique, since two full-dimensional compact
convex bodies differing as sets differ on positive volume.

If y=g_K then D=K. Otherwise the cut is proper, since a full cap would
have nonzero moment. Its boundary meets int K and its normalized hinge
parameter u_* is unique: different proper cutting planes have different
positive regions on an open part of int K.

In particular any convex cap with centroid y is this maximizing cap:
normalize its affine cutting function to take value one at y, which
is strictly inside that cap, and use its zero moment in the same proof.

## 2. The coupling and its equality information

We recall the actual conditional-quantile construction, including the
part needed for equality. No multivariate differentiability assumption
on the boundary is made. Full details of the construction are in
`candidate 4bb4c167681e8955`.

For a convex body D of volume v, the successive projection fiber
volumes W_j are positive and continuous on the interiors of their
projection domains. Continuity follows from ordinary Brunn--Minkowski
and concavity of their positive roots. Conditional cumulative
distribution functions, integrating W_j and dividing by W_(j-1),
are strictly increasing in their own coordinate. Their inverses define
a triangular homeomorphism X_D:(0,1)^d -> int D. Its positive own-
coordinate derivatives are continuous and satisfy

 b_(D,j)=partial_(u_j) X_(D,j)
         =W_(j-1)(X_<j)/W_j(X_<=j),
                  product_j b_(D,j)=v.                            (7)

The conditional interval endpoints are continuous on their interior
prefix domains; this follows from convexity/concavity of the lower and
upper endpoint functions. Thus the map and its inverse are continuous
by recursive bracketing. Repeated one-dimensional substitution gives

 integral_(image X) F(x)dx
    =integral_(0,1)^d F(X(u)) product_j partial_(u_j)X_j(u) du       (8)

for any such triangular map with positive own derivatives and any
nonnegative Borel F. This uses only Tonelli and one-dimensional
substitution, not unspecified cross derivatives. Equation (7) shows
that X_D sends uniform cube probability to uniform probability on D.
Convex-body boundaries are null, for example by inner homothety.

Apply these maps to D_i, write v_i=|D_i|, s_i=v_i^(1/d), and put

 Z(u)=sum_i lambda_i X_(D_i)(u),
 R=sum_i lambda_i s_i,   omega_i=lambda_i s_i/R.

This map is again triangular and injective, with continuous positive
own derivatives and continuous conditional endpoints. Its image G is
open and (8) applies. Its derivative product J obeys

 J/R^d=product_j sum_i omega_i [b_(D_i,j)/s_i]
       >=product_j product_i [b_(D_i,j)/s_i]^omega_i=1.             (9)

The inequality is the weighted arithmetic-geometric mean inequality in
each coordinate. Equality holds if and only if, for each j, the values
b_(D_i,j)/s_i are all identical across i. All weights are positive.

The law of Z has density 1/J(Z^(-1)(x)) on G and zero off G by (8).
Thus R^d Law(Z)<=1_K dx. Its mass is R^d, its mean is
sum_i lambda_i g_(D_i)=y, and its support lies in sum_i lambda_i D_i.
This proves (2), including the superbody version.

Suppose equality holds in (2). The last dominated density is an
optimizer in (1), so it equals 1_(D_K(y)) almost everywhere. Since
G is open, D_K(y) is closed, and the density is strictly positive on G,
we have G subset D_K(y), hence G subset int D_K(y). Consequently J=R^d
almost everywhere on the cube. Its continuity makes this equality
pointwise, and equality holds in every coordinate of (9).

This conclusion holds for a coupling constructed in ANY orthonormal
coordinate frame. Fix a unit vector u as its first axis. The first
coordinate of X_(D_i) is the projected quantile Q_i(r), 0<r<1. The
equalities in (9) give

                Q_i'(r)/s_i=Q_1'(r)/s_1.

Integrate, and determine the additive constant from the projected
means integral_0^1 Q_i(r)dr=u.y_i. It follows that

 (Q_i(r)-u.y_i)/s_i=(Q_1(r)-u.y_1)/s_1.                           (10)

Quantiles approach their finite support endpoints as r increases to
one. Thus (10) gives

 [h_(D_i)(u)-u.y_i]/s_i=[h_(D_1)(u)-u.y_1]/s_1

for every unit u. Equality of support functions proves D_i=y_i+s_iD_0
for one volume-one centroid-zero body D_0. Their Minkowski combination
D'=y+R D_0 lies in K, has centroid y and volume R^d. Its indicator is
another optimizer in (1); uniqueness gives D'=D_K(y). This proves
necessity in (4). Conversely (4) makes the target optimal volume R^d,
proving sufficiency. This completes the equality proof in every d>=1.

The repeated first-axis argument is essential: equality in one fixed
triangular frame alone would not justify removing possible shears.
These coordinate frames are used only inside ordinary continuous
fibers; no transformation of an integer lattice is made.

## 3. Strict quasiconcavity and continuity inside a body

Set T_i=T_K(y_i)>0 and t=min(T_1,T_2). The two densities

                    f_i=(t/T_i)1_(D_K(y_i))

lie between zero and one, have mass t, and have barycenters y_i.
Their convex combination is feasible with mass t at
y=(1-lambda)y_1+lambda y_2. If T_K(y)=t, uniqueness from Section 1
forces that combination to be the indicator of D_K(y). A strict convex
combination of two numbers in [0,1] equals zero or one only when both
numbers equal that same endpoint. Thus f_1=f_2=1_(D_K(y)) a.e.
Since t>0, this forces t/T_i=1, D_K(y_i)=D_K(y), and y_1=y_2.
This contradiction proves (5).

In particular T has a unique maximizer on any nonempty compact convex
subset of int K. It attains that maximum because T^(1/d) is finite
and concave on int K by (2) with K_1=K_2=K, and every finite concave
function is continuous on an open convex domain. The latter elementary
fact follows by bounding slopes on a small inner cube: concavity bounds
each inner secant between the slopes to the surrounding cube faces.

Boundary points have zero retained mass: a supporting linear function
nonnegative on K and vanishing at y has zero integral against any
feasible density, which is therefore supported on a null hyperplane.
No boundary value or boundary continuity is needed in Theorems A--B.

## 4. Exact contrast with projective energy

For the standard simplex K=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d), write V=|K| and g=g_K.
For y_t=tg, 0<t<=1, the actual cap tK has centroid y_t and hence is
the optimizer in Section 1. Thus

 T_K(y_t)=V t^d,          T_K(y_t)^(1/d)=V^(1/d)t.                 (11)

The exact simplex projective-energy formula, proved by the minimizing
projective map in the sharp comparison source, is

 E_K(y_t)=V t^d(d+1-dt),
 E_K(y_t)^(1/d)=V^(1/d)t(d+1-dt)^(1/d).                           (12)

The second derivative of the last scalar factor is

              -(d+1)(2-t)(d+1-dt)^(1/d-2)<0.                    (13)

So strict energy concavity does not transfer to strict retained-cap
root concavity. There is no conflict with (5), since T strictly
increases along the ray in (11).

## 5. Equality does not force whole-body homothety

In R^2 with coordinates (x,t), let

 C_infty={t<=1, |x|<=1-t},
 D=C_infty intersect {t>=0},
 K_1=C_infty intersect {t>=-1},
 K_2=K_1 intersect {x<=3/2}.

The body D is the triangle with vertices (0,1),(-1,0),(1,0), of area
one and centroid y=(0,1/3). The body K_1 is a triangle and K_2 is the
quadrilateral with vertices (0,1),(-2,-1),(3/2,-1),(3/2,-1/2).
Both have the actual centroidal cap D at t>=0, so T_(K_i)(y)=1.

For every 0<lambda<1, M=(1-lambda)K_1+lambda K_2 is contained in
C_infty and contains D. Since C_infty intersect {t>=0}=D, its same
cap is exactly D. Hence T_M(y)=1 and equality in (2) holds. The input
bodies are not homothetic: one has three extreme points, the other four.

Thus no whole-input equality or contact conclusion follows from
retained-cap equality alone. This example is not asserted to have
the displayed marks globally deepest for a mixed family. It refutes
the ordinary whole-body implication, precisely the step that equality
in (2) on its own would otherwise attempt to supply.

## 6. A physical retained-cap stratum on the actual deepest set

Here d>=1, n>=0, and C is an actual compact convex body in R^n x R^d
whose induced mixed set has positive mixed d-volume. Let P_0 be its
finite set of nonempty integer fibers K_p. Some K_p may have dimension
less than d. Define the finite measure

 mu(A)=sum_(p in P_0) |{x in K_p:(p,x) in A}|_d,
 Delta(Y)=inf{mu(H): H closed ambient halfspace, Y in H},
 beta=max_(Y in S) Delta(Y).

All halfspaces, including pure integer and oblique ones, are included.
The maximum exists and beta>0. Indeed S is compact. For Y_j->Y, any
closed halfspace H={a.Y>=b} containing Y can be replaced by
H_epsilon={a.Y>=b-epsilon}; all sufficiently late Y_j belong to it.
Thus limsup Delta(Y_j)<=mu(H_epsilon), which decreases to mu(H) as
epsilon decreases to zero. Infimizing over H proves upper
semicontinuity. Positivity follows by choosing the center of an inner
ball in any positive-volume fiber: every containing ambient halfspace
captures at least half that ball, or its whole fiber.

Every positive-depth point (p,y) lies in int K_p. Here is the precise
finite support argument, including zero-volume fibers. Choose a
continuous supporting unit normal u at a noninterior y of K_p, so
u.y=h_(K_p)(u). There is a finite vector A in R^n with

 h_(K_z)(u)<=h_(K_p)(u)+A.(z-p) for every z in P_0.                (14)

By finite Farkas, failure would give nonnegative numbers lambda_z
whose weighted base displacement is zero and whose weighted support
excess is positive. Normalize their sum to one. Actual convexity
gives sum lambda_z K_z subset K_p, contradicting that support excess.
The ambient halfspace

              u.x-A.(z-p)>=h_(K_p)(u)

contains (p,y) and cuts from each fiber at most a supporting face.
Every such face has d-volume zero, also for lower-dimensional fibers.
It therefore has mu-mass zero. This proves the claim. In particular
all deepest points lie in positive-dimensional interiors in the sense
int_(R^d) K_p, not on discarded lower-dimensional fibers.

Let Y={Y in S:Delta(Y)=beta}. It is a nonempty compact set. The
function (p,y)->T_(K_p)(y) is continuous on Y by Section 3 and the
finite number of fibers. Hence the following quantities are attained:

 tau=max_(Y in Y) T_(K_p)(y)>0,
 Y_tau={(p,y) in Y:T_(K_p)(y)=tau}.                              (15)

**Theorem C.** The set Y_tau has at most one point at each integer
base. If (p_i,y_i) in Y_tau, lambda_i>0 sum to one, and
p=sum lambda_i p_i is integral, then

 (p,sum lambda_i y_i) in Y_tau,
 D_(K_pi)(y_i)=y_i+D_0 for one common centroid-zero body D_0,
 D_(K_p)(sum lambda_i y_i)=sum lambda_i D_(K_pi)(y_i).             (16)

The common D_0 in (16) has volume tau. Consequently the selected base
set U=projection(Y_tau) is lattice-complete in conv(U), and at most
2^n translation classes of selected retained caps occur.

Proof. The deepest points in one fiber form a convex set: any closed
halfspace containing a convex combination of two such points contains
at least one of them, and hence has mass at least beta. Its depth
equals beta by global maximality. If two distinct such points both
maximized T, (5) would yield a deeper-stratum point with larger T,
contradiction. This proves the first assertion.

For the barycentric statement, actual convexity puts the displayed
point in K_p. Any halfspace containing it contains one of the finitely
many (p_i,y_i); therefore it too is deepest. Inequality (2) gives
T_(K_p)(sum lambda_i y_i)>=tau, while (15) gives the reverse inequality.
Equality classification (4), with all input cap volumes equal to tau,
proves (16). Every integer point of conv(U) has such a finite convex
representation, after dropping zero weights. Thus it belongs to U.
Finally two selected bases in the same parity class have an integral
midpoint, so (16) makes their retained caps translates. Each occupied
parity class supplies at most one translation class, proving the bound.

## 7. Exact limitations of the mixed structural conclusion

Theorem C controls one positive physical cap per selected point. It
does not compare tau, the sum of their volumes, or their overlaps with
the original mass mu(S). It does not assert whole-fiber homothety,
free perturbability of the caps, a cap cover of S, or a global affine
graph of selected marks. Those would require separate arguments.

The last graph limitation is realized exactly. Take n=2,d=1, bases
P={0,1}^2, and length-two intervals K_p=[c_p-1,c_p+1], with
c_(0,0)=c_(1,0)=c_(0,1)=0 and c_(1,1)=1. Let C be the convex hull of
these four vertical intervals. It is a full-dimensional convex body,
and its only integer fibers are the four displayed intervals. At each
fiber midpoint, every containing ambient halfspace captures at least
one unit from its own interval. Conversely a finite base tilt exposing
that square vertex excludes all other fibers and leaves the shorter
own interval tail. Thus raw depth at (p,x) is exactly

                         1-|x-c_p|.

All four midpoints are the unique deepest points; their T values are
two, so Y_tau is exactly their graph. That graph is nonaffine. There
are no nontrivial integer anchors between different vertices of the
hollow square, so this example fully respects (16).

For d=0, T^(1/d) is undefined and is not invoked. Purely atomic
centerpoint arguments belong to a separate case. Nothing here claims
a new intrinsic-q extension with changing affine fiber directions.
Theorem C explicitly assumes positive mixed d-volume (q=d), while
retaining all nonempty lower-dimensional boundary fibers in its
compactness and zero-depth arguments.

## 8. A successive physical-mass and energy refinement

There is a useful refinement, not a mass-payment conclusion. On the
finite nonempty set Y_tau, maximize the ordinary projective energy E:

 e=max_(p,y in Y_tau) E_(K_p)(y),
 Z={(p,y) in Y_tau:E_(K_p)(y)=e}.                                 (17)

This second maximum is attained. The audited theorem in
`candidate 5811f0ad1132ce56`,
Section 7, states that E^(1/d) is jointly Minkowski concave with equality
only for positively homothetic MARKED whole bodies. It is also strictly
increasing under a proper full-dimensional body inclusion at a fixed
interior mark: evaluate the target's attained positive-denominator
integral on the smaller body and its positive-volume difference.
The first part is at least the smaller optimum and the difference is
strictly positive. Hence superbody equality also forces exact inclusion.

If selected points of Z have an integer-anchored barycentric combination,
Section 6 puts the combined point in Y_tau. Joint energy concavity gives
its energy at least e; maximality in (17) gives equality. The marked
homotheties have equal energies, so their scale factors are all one.
Consequently, for a single marked body L,

 K_(p_i)=y_i+L for every input i,
 K_p=(sum_i lambda_i y_i)+L.                                    (18)

Thus Z remains integer-anchored closed and supplies whole-fiber marked-
translation rigidity under its actual anchored relations, while also
preserving the maximal retained mass tau. There are again at most 2^n
marked whole-fiber translation classes, by taking same-parity midpoints.
Neither (17) nor (18) supplies exhaustion or coverage of the original
mixed mass. In particular the hollow-square example in Section 7 still
prevents a global affine graph inference.

## 9. Supplementary exact verification

`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_physical_centroidal_cap_concavity_two_sided.py` passes 3,138
exact checks. It reconstructs every rational Minkowski polygon in the
tail example for denominators through forty, verifies its actual cap,
checks the symbolic derivative (13), and certifies the finite isolating
tilts in the nonaffine hollow-square example. These checks supplement,
and do not replace, the preceding proofs.
